Abu Dhabi markets itself to global elites—can its public art biennial reach local communities?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The arrival of Frieze furthers Abu Dhabi’s ambitions to become a premier events destination for global elites.
  • But a glittering trail of franchised events is unlikely to leave a lasting impact on the local communities that have built Abu Dhabi and will continue to sustain it.
  • According to recent reports, public art appears to be one strategy, so proposes the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial (until 15 February 2027).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The arrival of Frieze furthers Abu Dhabi’s ambitions to become a premier events destination for global elites. Beyond the fair (which runs until 22 November), the coming weeks will see the jetset descend on the emirate to bid on Picassos at Sotheby’s, sit front row at the Grand Prix and Abu Dhabi Open tournaments, and rub shoulders with celebrities and chief executives at the Global Cultural Forum and the Milken Institute's Middle East and Africa Summit.

But a glittering trail of franchised events is unlikely to leave a lasting impact on the local communities that have built Abu Dhabi and will continue to sustain it. Focusing efforts on attracting the itinerant super-rich might also prove short-sighted for a country surrounded by well-armed and hostile neighbours. So, how to engage those who will remain when regional conflicts escalate or the markets turn?

According to recent reports, public art appears to be one strategy, so proposes the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial (until 15 February 2027). Organised by the Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT), the exhibition Home: A Glossary for a Communal Sense of Place has brought 18 works—most of them fresh commissions—to public sites across the city, with a further four situated in the nearby oasis desert town of Al Ain.

Asunción Molinos Gordo, Bil Hana wa Al Afia (2026), installation view, Al Ain.Image courtesy of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Department of Culture and Tourism— Abu Dhabi.

“Everyday life is central” to this biennial “both as backdrop and method”, writes its artistic director, Elvira Dyangani Ose, in the accompanying guide. Out in the desert, Iron Age irrigation systems still used today form the basis of Ascunción Molinos Gordo’s rammed earth sculpture Bil Hana wa Al Afia (2026), installed among working farms during the biennial’s run. Back in the city, the ubiquitous infrastructure of cooling vents is brought to the fore by Shama Al Hamed’s installation of fluorescent aluminium ducting, which spill out like entrails from the observation deck of the former industrial port.

Recent findings suggest that key to a public art biennial concerned with the quotidian is appealing to non-art specialist audiences. This means considering the “many publics” that exist in Abu Dhabi, Dyangani Ose says. Visitors at sunset will see families jumping on Ivan Argote’s see-saw installation and zooming down its animal-shaped slides.

Sources indicate that despite the temporary nature of an exhibition, each edition of the biennial achieves permanence through its acquisition structure. Last edition, 15 works—around half—were acquired by Public Art Abu Dhabi and are now on display across the city. They include a crescent of silver oyster sculptures by the Emirati artist Farah Al Qasimi, referencing the Arabian Gulf’s once-booming pearl diving industry.

Sources indicate that the director of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Clémence Bergal, indicates a similar acquisition round will take place at the end of this edition. “With so many of the biennial’s works being upcoming commissions, it is a great way to collect work that feels deeply connected and responsive to Abu Dhabi,” she says.

Elvira Dyangani Ose, artistic director of the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial.

In a recent development, the biennial is not only a tool for engaging Abu Dhabi’s various communities, but for considering how they live with each other. The theme of this year is the unstable and contested definition of “home”, and Dyangani Ose writes in the catalogue that she is interested in how a “communal sense of place” is formed and negotiated by various groups, sometimes of vastly different cultures and material conditions. “Abu Dhabi is a city in which that distinction matters enormously,” she writes. “Communities from across the world share its streets, its coastline, its daily rhythms without sharing the same histories, the same rights or the same relationship to the land.”.

The curatorial statement provides a potent line of inquiry in a country where only a small portion of the population—estimated to be around 12%—has citizenship, and in which the working and living conditions of migrant labourers has been criticised by leading human rights organisations.

Sources indicate that these issues appear to be broached obliquely in the multiple references to migration and labour throughout the biennial, including in a striking coastline installation by the Ghanaian artist Serge Attukwei Clottey, composed of thousands of interlocking yellow plastic pieces made from Kuffuor gallons—containers that are ubiquitous in Accra and used to transport cooking oil, water and fuel. These Kuffuor installations are Clottey’s signature, and he has spoken widely about how they refer, in part, to the imbalanced relations of labour and resource extraction between African nations and their trading partners. The UAE is Ghana’s third-most important importer, chiefly purchasing gold. Immigrants from Ghana and other West African nations represent an increasingly large portion of the UAE's manual labour force, chiefly working in construction, hospitality and security services.

Yinka Shonibare, Wind Sculpture (TG) III (2026), installationview, Abu Dhabi, 2026.

Image courtesy of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Department of Culture and Tourism— Abu Dhabi.

Industry observers note that unsurprisingly considering the emirate's strict censorship laws, little in the show could be openly perceived as critical, at least of the UAE. Dyangani Ose tells The Art Newspaper that there are certain “limits presented by the framework” of a publicly funded exhibition in Abu Dhabi. She adds that "as global subjects", we are all bound within certain limits.

To its credit, the biennial's public setting provides opportunities for conversations that many art institutions in other parts of the world might shy away from. For instance, Yinka Shonibare’s towering metal plume, painted in both his signature Dutch wax patterns and those of Bedouin textiles, serves as a welcome shade structure for outdoor labourers working in the harsh midday sun. "These publics are just as vital to take into account as any other," Dyangani Ose indicates.

According to recent reports, indeed, providing a platform for a diverse and unexpected set of interactions is a vital part of how Dyangani Ose conceives of a communal sense of place, as “making meaning, despite differences, in public”. For the biennial, this might be its greatest impact of all.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Design Museum.

Ten leading designers have unveiled posters that celebrate 10 years of London’s Design Museum in Kensington, which was completed by OMA, Allies and Morrison and John Pawson in 2016.

Originally located in an old 1940s banana warehouse on the south bank of the River Thames, the Design Museum opened at its current site in Kensington, west London, on 24 November 2016.

To mark this 10-year anniversary, the museum asked 10 international designers to create posters for the occasion.

The lineup includes British graphic designer Margaret Calvert, who is known for creating the seminal 1960s Motorway and Transport typefaces with fellow British designer Jock Kinneir.

The hugely popular typefaces were invented to clarify the UK’s road signs and are still used today.

Calvert designed a subtle road sign-style poster for the Design Museum’s anniversary, depicting a fork in the road between Kensington and Shad Thames, where the original museum stood between 1989 and 2016.

Former Apple designer Jony Ive also conceived a poster in collaboration with his studio LoveFrom, which he founded with Australian practitioner Marc Newson in 2019 after his departure from the technology brand.

Ive and LoveFrom‘s poster features a minimalist grey and white design composed of two understated shapes that resemble the number 10.

American filmmaker Tim Burton is also among the lineup and applied his trademark playful drawings to a poster illustrated with two characters sitting atop the number 10.

Burton’s extensive portfolio was on display at the Design Museum in 2024, charting 50 years of his cinematic career.

Dutch industrial designer Hella Jongerius, meanwhile, created a poster depicting a colourful woven tapestry in a nod to her work, which typically blends contemporary technology with traditional crafts.

The other six designers who make up the lineup are London studio A Practice for Everyday Life, Brazilian graphic designer Marina Willer, British fashion designer Paul Smith and British designers Sebastian Conran, Simone Brewster and Tom Dixon.

The Kensington Design Museum is located within the former Commonwealth Institute building.

Dutch architecture practice OMA worked alongside London office Allies and Morrison to restore the shell of the Grade II*-listed building, while British designer Pawson conceived the museum’s interiors.

Images courtesy of Design Museum.

  • A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists. The technology works as specified. However, the specialists stop using it, and the ones who keep using it take longer on each case than the ones who ignore it.

According to recent reports, A short evaluation with the specialists surfaces the problem fast: reading an AI-written determination carefully enough to sign it takes about as long as writing one, and the specialist also has to check for mistakes they would never have made themselves. The feature adds work to a task these people had already mastered.

In a recent development, rescoping the release fixes it. A second version surfaces the policy provisions and prior decisions relevant to each appeal and leaves the writing to the specialist. The search step disappears, review time drops, and the part of the job the specialist is good at stays where it was.

The technology is identical in both versions, and the difference is which part of the task the AI handles.

In a recent development, every interface change costs the user something before it pays anything back. They have to rebuild their picture of how the tool works, learn where things are now, and decide how far to trust what the AI hands them. Nelson Cowan’s review of working memory research (2001) put the limit at about four items held in mind at once. All three of those jobs draw on the same small supply.

Recent findings suggest that an AI feature in an enterprise software setting requires more from the user than a redesigned menu, because it changes what they do all day. Hand the synthesis to an AI and the user becomes a checker. Give it the recommendation too, and the job shrinks to signing off. Either change costs user attention, and for people whose training is their standing at work, either one can feel like a demotion. For example, in one study, Sophia Ackerhans (2025) and colleagues found that physicians asked to sign AI-assisted decisions reported a more serious threat to their professional identity, and explanations of the AI’s reasoning raised both trust and that threat together.

It has been revealed that we can call that the break-even line. Returns to users come in three forms:.

For example, an AI-powered fraud screening tool indicates the errors-caught form at work, since the analyst reviews flags they would never have raised themselves, which costs attention, and the catch rate pays for it. That puts the feature above the break-even line.

Four questions can help your team locate the break-even line before design work starts. Each one produces a design condition the brief can act on.

These questions do not replace the build decision. Funding, strategy, and existing commitments all weigh on that, and four questions cannot see any of it.

Run through all four questions together, since no single question settles the issue alone. Do it while the feature is still a proposal, before anyone sinks weeks into design. You will also need at least one person who does the task for a living, such as a loan officer, analyst, or benefits specialist. They do not have to sit in the roadmap meeting, and a short conversation tells you where the mental effort actually sits and whether the feature would help or add work.

Recent findings suggest that count everything the task asks of the user: the thinking, the clicking, and the checking they will owe once AI is involved. Fewer clicks proves nothing on its own, because a feature can cut clicks and still leave the person working harder. Write down the cost even when it goes up, since Question 2 may find a return that pays for it.

According to recent reports, A loan officer reading 40 financial disclosures to find the three that conflict with lending policy is thinking hard, and AI that surfaces those conflicts cuts that demand directly. Compare that with typing a loan number into a tracking system, which costs a few seconds and almost no thought. Pre-filling that field relocates the cost instead of removing it, because the officer now checks what the machine entered. Conventional wisdom states to automate the repetitive and monotonous tasks, and the pre-filled field is where that advice misfires. In this example:.

You can find the tasks worth automating by comparing total effort before and after. Count the checking the user inherits on the after side.

In a recent development, who the user is matters as much as what the task is. One feature can clear the line for a junior analyst and fall short for a senior one. Hand a junior analyst an AI-drafted risk summary, and they gain a starting point they lack the pattern library to produce on their own. A senior analyst, however, reads that same summary against the analysis already formed in their head, spends four minutes doing it, and learns nothing.

Industry observers note that A finding like that tells you who to ship to. Scope the addition to the group it serves.

Industry observers note that compare the AI approach against the user’s current method, including the spreadsheets and workarounds they built for themselves. Genuine ambiguity is one reason AI comes out ahead when someone explores options, produces a starting point, or looks for patterns too numerous to spot by hand. Scale, speed, and consistency across a group of people doing the same job are three more. A fourth is catching what the current method reliably misses, which is how the fraud screening tool earns its place. The advantage disappears once the user has a practiced route to a known answer.

Recent findings suggest that for example, an HR team building a succession planning tool finds the answer running both ways inside one product. Using AI to surface internal candidates whose skill combinations nobody would think to search for wins on ambiguity and scale together, since no single right answer exists and manual review of that search space would take weeks. Drafting the notification email after someone picks a candidate loses to the method already in place. The format is familiar, the writing takes two minutes, and the person sending it holds firm opinions about tone. The candidate search earns the addition. The email draft layers an interaction onto a task that runs fine without one.

Industry observers note that the nature of the input and the shape of the output are separate decisions. A task can hold genuine ambiguity and still call for a structured visual result instead of a conversational one. Pair this audit with a modality evaluation for the output side.

In a recent development, every AI system makes mistakes. The question is whether your user will notice. Start with how visible the error is. Then weigh what it costs when nobody catches it, and whether the user still has the skill to catch it. Question 1 asks what checking costs. This one asks whether checking is even possible.

Industry observers note that error visibility varies enormously, and product teams tend to estimate it badly. For example, an AI trip planner that suggests a museum on the day it closes produces an invisible error, because nothing in the output looks wrong. The traveler finds out while standing outside a locked door in Tokyo. Compare that with a suggested flight that departs before the connecting flight lands, where the contradiction sits right there on the screen.

Recent findings suggest that automation bias makes the invisible cases worse. Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey (2010) reviewed decades of human factors research showing that people defer to automated output even when that output is wrong, across aviation, medicine, and process control. Trust climbs fast, and rarely as a conscious decision. Once it does, people stop applying the scrutiny that would catch the mistake.

Industry observers note that map the error surface, meaning the ways this feature can be wrong, before design work starts. List the three likeliest error types. Rate each one on visibility to the user and consequence if it slips through. Any combination of low visibility and high consequence becomes a design requirement.

In a recent development, show users where the output came from and how the system produced it. That is provenance, and it is what lets trust settle at the right level. People who can see the source, the data behind it, and when it was pulled catch errors more often. Tell the traveler that a restaurant’s hours came from a page cached in March and they know what to check. A confident-sounding paragraph with no source attached leaves them guessing.

Letting the routine work go is a real benefit of adding AI. Nobody needs to protect a specialist’s ability to format a citation or an analyst’s ability to total a column by hand, and arguing to preserve skills the technology has absorbed wastes everyone’s time.

According to recent reports, still, the judgment that catches the machine’s mistakes stays exempt from replacement. That judgment makes every other delegation safe, and disuse degrades it like any other skill.

Research in radiology reveals how fast a suggestion can override a reader’s own judgment. In a 2023 experiment, Thomas Dratsch and colleagues had 27 radiologists read mammograms alongside what they were told was an AI system (a simulation created solely for the experiment). The radiologists worked through a 10-image training set where the suggested category was always correct, then 40 more mammograms with incorrect suggestions planted in 12 of them. The result demonstrated how incorrect AI suggestions damaged diagnostic accuracy at every experience level. The most experienced readers, averaging 15 years, assigned the correct category 82.3% of the time when the suggestion was right and 45.5% of the time when it was wrong, while the least experienced group fell from 79.7% to 19.8%. Experience softened the effect without preventing it. A year of deferring to the same system, with the judgment it replaced sitting unused, leaves a reader in a weaker position than the one these radiologists started from.

Sources indicate that question 3 looks at your user today. Extend the same test 12 months forward and you arrive at Question 4. Teams that answer the first and skip the second read the resulting failures as a quality problem in the model, when the cause is the human judgment they took out of daily use.

It has been revealed that ask whether this user could judge the quality of the output 12 months from now if the feature vanished tomorrow. When the answer is no, the design needs a mechanism that keeps verification skill in use. Periodic blind review works well and costs little, with the user forming a judgment before seeing what the AI produced. Rotating a share of cases off AI assistance does a similar job, as does a weekly comparison between machine output and a human-produced version.

Table 1 below gathers the four questions, the signals pointing each way, and the condition each one produces.

According to recent reports, table 1: The AI Addition Decision Matrix. Clear answers across all four questions point toward building the feature as proposed. A poor answer on Question 1 calls for a design condition or a change in scope, unless Question 2 finds a return that covers the cost. Questions 2 and 4 work the same way without that exception. A poor answer on Question 3 can stop the build.

Put the conditions in the design brief, where they become project requirements. Teams reduce AI features to yes or no because roadmap reviews demand it, and that throws away everything the audit found. A feature that answers well on Questions 1 and 2 and poorly on Question 3 proceeds only with provenance built in. Write that in on day one. Requirements that arrive at the end read as polish, and teams cut polish when timelines slip.

Sources indicate that let’s return to the insurer scenario from our opening. The first version of the tool fails Question 1. Writing a determination takes sustained thought, and the AI that produces the draft moves that effort into verification without reducing the total. An hour with the four questions would surface that before the first version reaches design.

Question 2 points in the same direction. Appeals determinations follow a familiar structure, and specialists reach the answer through a practiced route. The ambiguity in the task sits earlier, in finding which provisions and prior decisions apply.

Industry observers note that question 3 raises the stakes. A wrong determination affects someone’s medical coverage, and an error buried in fluent prose stays invisible until the next appeal arrives. That answer produces the provenance requirement in the second version, which cites the source document and retrieval date for every provision it surfaces.

It has been revealed that question 4 explains why the second version holds up. Specialists still write every determination, so the judgment that evaluates the retrieved material stays in daily use. Keeping version one would train specialists for a year to approve text they no longer have the practice to assess.

AI-generated meeting summaries sit inside products that millions of people open every day, and the audit reaches a different answer for them.

On Question 1, a summary removes the work of writing notes and adds the work of checking whether it attributed a decision to the right person. Total effort drops for the participant who never took notes. For the person who always took the notes and circulated them, the trade is closer, and the verification lands on them. That split is exactly what Question 1 is built to surface.

Sources indicate that question 2 compares the summary against someone typing while half-listening, which produces patchy notes. A summary beats that on completeness and on consistency from meeting to meeting, so the feature clears this question for most teams.

A summary that assigns a commitment to the wrong person looks exactly like a correct one, and nobody rereads the transcript to check. On Question 3, low visibility and real consequence together turn into a requirement for a linked source timestamp behind every action item.

According to recent reports, the feature clears Question 4, and the design needs no mechanism. Nobody loses a skill worth protecting by giving up meeting notes, and the participants keep making every decision the summary records.

According to recent reports, two clear answers, one segment finding, and one condition. The timestamps ship with the feature, and the habitual note-taker is the segment the team checks after launch.

You can run this before the next AI feature reaches your roadmap.

In a recent development, everett Rogers (2003) called this pro-innovation bias, the assumption that newly introduced capability means progress before anyone verifies the benefit, and competitive pressure turns a rival’s announcement into an internal mandate. An hour of structured questions gives your team a way to answer that pressure.

Recent findings suggest that audit results land badly when a designer presents them as reasons the feature should not exist. The conditions are the useful output, so bring those into the product review.

Start by naming the segment the feature serves, which makes the answer a yes for someone. Hand over the error surface as a requirement with a cost attached. A product manager can act on a request for timestamps behind every attributed decision, and nobody can act on a worry that people might not trust the output. Then offer the change in scope without waiting to be asked. A version that surfaces the provisions instead of writing the determination is a smaller build with a better adoption story, and that framing moves a roadmap conversation forward.

A sentence that works out loud: We think this clears the bar for junior analysts and adds a verification step for senior analysts, so we would scope it to onboarding and revisit the rest next quarter.

It has been revealed that the attention a person can spend in a working day stays fixed no matter how good your model gets. Before the next feature reaches design, write down what it will cost the person doing the work and which of the three returns pays for it. With both answers in hand, your team can walk into the roadmap review with a scope to propose.

Sources indicate that lately, I’ve been thinking and writing a lot about what AI is doing to product development, and what that means for accessibility. The thing that has my wheels turning is a finding from Level Access’s 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. Basically: AI is helping us hit fast-forward on the build, but testing practices haven’t kept up.

We asked more than 2,500 professionals where they noticed AI was speeding up their work in the SDLC. Most said they noticed gains in planning (58%), design (61%), and development (51%). But QA and testing lagged behind: Only 30% said AI had sped up that stage.

These results point to a two-speed workflow. AI has turbocharged design, planning, and development, while checking and validation are still running at a very different pace. This means a lot of teams are likely racing through the build, then being forced to hit the brakes the moment someone has to answer a pretty fundamental question: Is this thing actually accessible?

Accessibility has historically been treated as a QA bottleneck, and AI is pushing far more work into it, faster. If your team has already shifted left on accessibility, you’re off to a good start. But AI has reshuffled the workflow, so even proactive teams need to work out where those early checks belong now.

This matters because right now, the web is moving in the wrong direction. WebAIM’s latest scan of the top million home pages found that automatically detected errors per home page rose 10.1% in a year, from 51 to 56.1 per page. WebAIM cited AI-assisted coding as one possible contributing factor.

So how do we get validation out of first gear? How do we build human judgment into the workflow as AI keeps pushing the pace?

We looked at the organizations that are improving across every accessibility metric they track (a group we call the “improvers”) to find out what they’re doing differently.

Here’s what stood out: AI adoption made the smallest difference of anything we measured. Improvers use AI at a similar rate to everyone else we surveyed. Their edge reveals up in the maturity of their surrounding accessibility practices — things like training, communication, and a culture of accessibility.

Industry observers note that A quick caveat: This is survey data, so it only shows correlation, and mature programs may simply be better at tracking and reporting their wins. Even so, this finding was hard to ignore.

In a recent development, and it got even more interesting. Professionals in mature accessibility programs were nearly six times as likely to say AI helps them prioritize issues. They were also nearly three times as likely to say it helps them tackle accessibility more proactively in development.

In other words, AI works best as an amplifier of a strong program. With context, testing, environments, and guardrails in place, agents can take on a large share of the work from drafting through to operations, and much of the time lost to waiting and handoffs goes away. People stay responsible for deciding what to build and for approving what ships.

So let me ask you: When it comes to accessibility, where does human judgment sit in your workflow today?

Not sure? Here’s a quick way to find out.

Pick a feature you shipped recently and trace it from the first Figma frame to production. Mark every moment a person decided whether it would work for someone using a keyboard, a screen reader, or their browser at 400% zoom.

Sources indicate that how many marks did you get? If most of them cluster at the end of creation, you’re likely heading to one of two places: You’ll either ship accessibility barriers or spend the time you saved upstream fixing them later, when they’re harder and costlier to fix.

Here’s how to avoid both outcomes by building the right accessibility checks and judgment calls into the work your team is already doing.

As AI takes on more work, people need to stay involved at three points: finding complications, fixing them, and documenting the evidence. Each one plugs into a step your team already takes, like a handoff, a pull request, or a review, so nothing newly introduced gets added to the timeline, and accessibility keeps pace with the work that’s in motion.

Context fades fast. Put the first judgment checkpoints as close to the creation work as you can:.

Found the issue? Great. Fix it while it’s fresh. When challenges end up as tickets, make sure the context travels with them. They should carry the element, the repro, the related WCAG criterion, a suggested fix, and the PR link, so context doesn’t leak.

The worst time to start gathering evidence is when somebody’s asking for it.

Industry observers note that every check, fix, and judgment call throughout the process described above should ideally leave a trail. A fix isn’t done until something fails if the concern comes back. Ask your AI assistant to write the regression test with the fix and put the finding link and any judgment call in the PR description. That’s the receipt.

A passing test shows a known issue hasn’t returned. It doesn’t show the experience works. For what automation can’t cover, add a short note to the PR: what you tested, with which assistive technology, and any judgment calls you made.

AI has given digital creation a speed boost, but broadly speaking, validating the work hasn’t kept pace. Closing that gap isn’t about adopting more AI in more places or abandoning the toolset that helped make your team faster.

According to our data, the opportunity in front of teams is to build the practice around that toolset, so that human judgment is flagged, embedded, and acted on earlier, and more often.

We’ve only scratched the surface of what our data tells us about AI and accessibility. If you’re curious about what else we found, check out the 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. There’s plenty more to unpack.

Eight furniture designs informed by life in Upcoming York City

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Furniture designers contend with their personal experiences living in Upcoming York City through the objects in our most recent roundup.

Fresh York, New York has inspired filmmakers, writers and artists to make work since the city’s inception, and for designers, it’s no different.

The furniture and objects below explore aspects of moving to or living in New York City, whether it’s the difficulty of maintaining a career and community, the dissonance of missing home, the architecture, or dead, smooshed rats on the daily commute.

In many cases, the collections reflect on the designer’s own identities and heritages.

These include pieces by Kim Mupungilaï, Rafael Prieto and studio Tian & Teague, all of whom have lived or passed through New York during their practice.

Read on below to see how the metropolis has shaped their work.

What Still Holds, by Bechara Maalouf.

Bechara Maalouf created a series of lamps made out of wooden beams from Lower East Side buildings and intricate screens informed by the window guards at his family home in Lebanon.

The series, first displayed during NYC design week 2026 in May, merged Maalouf’s two homes as the designer grappled with the impacts of Israel’s ground invasion of Lebanon from afar.

Find out more about What Still Holds ›.

Pax New Yorkea, by Massimiliano Malagò.

Designer Massimiliano Malagò created an acrylic chair, covered in his own writings, that explores the challenges of maintaining a life in New York City.

“For me, this was making an object that is incredibly luxurious, incredibly grand, but it’s actually talking about something quite common and sometimes quite sad, because the hardships that people go through to stay in the city are just difficult,” he told Dezeen.

Find out more about Pax New Yorkea ›.

Los Angeles and Lisbon studio Tian & Teague created the NYC Series based on their own time living in Upcoming York and some of the jarring aspects residents become accustomed to.

The collection, which includes a flattened-rat rug, came about from things seen on the studio founders’ daily commute.

Find out more about NYC Series ›.

White Picket Chair, by Han Seungmin.

Fresh York-based designer Han Seungmin created this chair using modular components from the metallic fences found throughout Brooklyn.

First mass-produced in China in the 1980s, the fences are often used in Asian communities around the boroughs, and Han challenged “the idyllic image of the ‘American Dream’ from an immigrant perspective” through the piece.

Find out more about White Picket Chair ›.

HUE/AM/I-HUE/I/AM, by Kim Mupungilaï.

Belgian interior designer Kim Mupungilaï was prompted to design this collection of wood and fibre furniture after a 2018 visit to Fresh York that inspired her to explore her half-Belgian, half-Congolese roots.

“I just started thinking about my own cultural landscape and background and upbringing and wanted to dig deeper,” Mupungilaï told Dezeen.

Find out more about HUE/AM/I-HUE/I/AM ›.

The City Block, by Micah Rosenblatt.

Metalworker and designer Micah Rosenblatt looked to New York City’s historic architecture for his The City Block collection, which features thin, contemporary lines and geometric elements.

Recent findings suggest that “[The expressions] are based on the cityscape and my relationship to it,” Rosenblatt told Dezeen. “It’s the forms that you would look out and see on your horizon via whatever time period you’re in.”.

Find out more about The City Block ›.

All Other Passports, by Julio Torres and Sabai.

Comedian and actor Julio Torres worked with furniture manufacturer Sabai to create his first furniture collection, All Other Passports, debuted during NYC design week 2026.

The collection is influenced by literal and figurative aspects of Torres’ move to Latest York City from El Salvador, such as a curtain motif pulled from JFK‘s international Terminal 4.

Find out more about All Other Passports ›.

For The Future of the Past, by Rafael Prieto.

Designer Rafael Prieto integrated building fragments into several furniture pieces for an exhibition at Emma Scully Gallery earlier this year.

Prieto sourced the cast-offs, including pieces of a cornice, from a facade being demolished across the street from his Tribeca studio, which he had become “deeply interested” in.

Find out more about For The Future of the Past ›.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the international photography museum Fotografiska has recently debuted in Shenzhen, its second space in mainland China, after Fotografiska Shanghai opened in 2023. “The strategy was always to self-fund the first space in Shanghai, and then expand through strategic partnerships for subsequent locations,” says Christian Devillers, the managing director for Fotografiska China.

The organisation, founded in Stockholm in 2010, also currently has locations in the Swedish capital, Fresh York, Berlin and Tallinn; and a new venue, in Oslo, is scheduled to open in 2028.

Sources indicate that “Museum-going culture [in Shenzhen] isn’t as deeply entrenched as it is in Shanghai or Hong Kong,” Devillers states, and its art-going demographic skews heavily toward young families and professionals. Fotografiska Shenzhen is replicating Shanghai’s late hours and lifestyle offerings, which draw office workers commuting to the city centres, and its first public day on the 1 October national holiday drew more than 1,000 paying visitors.

The project opened with exhibitions across the 5,300 sq. m facility, including a Shi Guowei solo show and Toiletpaper, showcasing Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari’s titular magazine (both until 14 March 2027). They have joined a show of photography award Prix Pictet (until 29 November), the six-artist group show Transcendent Realities (until 1 October 2027) and a Michael Najjar solo exhibition (until 17 January 2027). Subsequent planned events include a show of Hong Kong photographers featuring, among others, Ho Fan (1931-2016).

In Shanghai, even with Fotografiska’s busy traffic, admissions and memberships account for only around 20% of total revenue, Devillers says. The museum instead depends on commercial partnerships, and retail and food and drink sales. Fotografiska Shenzhen’s six-year partnership agreement with landlord China Resources Land aims to draw a profit by year three. The institution has set an initial target of 70,000 visitors for 2027.

It has been revealed that fotografiska Shenzhen is located in the upscale retail complex Shenzhen Bay MixC, which is also home to a latest immersive art concept called Base. They join several new and forthcoming cultural projects in the city, which is making a concerted push to raise its artistic profile, such as the recently-opened Shenzhen International Art Museum and Shenzhen Bay Cultural Plaza. This month will also see the long-running Hong Kong fair Fine Art Asia relocate to the mainland city (26-29 November).

BUCK gives conservation nonprofit Tula Global a brand identity built on a pixel spark, topographic lines and vivid color.

Headlines run large in the same rounded grotesque, set tight in short lines that stack like the pixel blocks, and the line that carries the whole offer reads plain: Six months. Real skills. Direct pathways to employment.

In a recent development, small caps kickers label each section, THE TULA MODEL, OUR GRADUATES, OUR MISSION, in a lighter weight that lets the significant lines breathe. The symbol grid becomes the layout grid. Panels split into halves and thirds along the same pixel rhythm, contour lines run across the joins, and the custom data visualizations sit inside the same structure, so a deck slide and a poster share one set of rules.

In a recent development, the system earns its keep in the field. Outdoor signs carry the wordmark and the mission in orange and cream, framed posters hang on brick, and the Tula Model booklet pairs green hills with lime contour lines. The mark travels just as well on cloth, embroidered in orange thread on a burgundy cap and printed large on the back of a field vest, then out to a white van running the green wordmark down its flank.

According to recent reports, on screen the same language holds, with the model page stacking major type, field photography and contour panels on a phone. Documentary photography of the training and the survey work sits beside the graphics rather than under them, and the custom data system turns the program into charts and maps that read at a glance. Nothing in the kit is decoration. Every panel, poster and garment repeats the grid, the lines and the color, so the identity feels built, not applied.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dinamo rebuilt early-web Arial from scratch for Are.na, turning invisible typography craft into ABC Areal and releasing the family free.

Are.na spent a full year rewriting its back-end code without changing a single visible pixel on screen. Nobody noticed, and nobody sent congratulations, yet Are.naâs Cab told Dinamoâs Johannes there was real satisfaction in fixing what sits underneath. That quiet pride sparked a tricky typography brief. Are.na had used Arial for fifteen years and didnât want a dramatic fresh voice; the default sans still felt like a less snobby cousin to Helvetica. Their breakthrough came from Kristin Lucasâs performance piece Refresh, in which she legally changed her own name to the exact same name just to start over. Berlin-based foundry Dinamo took that cue literally and redrew Arial from the ground up as ABC Areal â releasing the entire family for free one year after it went live on Are.na.

It has been revealed that unlike print revivals pulled from old books or posters, Arial was born digital. Commissioned by IBM in 1982 from Monotype designers Robin Nicholas and Patricia Saunders, it landed on Windows 3.1 in 1992 before Microsoft picked Arial 2.82 in 1996 as a core web font. Dinamo treated that thirty-year-old software like a dig site, partnering with technology archivists to boot legacy machines and capture screenshots of the original web release as a tracing blueprint. The payoff highlights immediately in the side-by-side lowercase a outline chart. Arial 2.82 packs clustered, uneven anchor points along its upper arch and bowl, whereas Areal 1.0 strips that clutter down to clean BÃ©zier extrema without disturbing the familiar slanted top terminal. Those rebuilt forms play out across four retro Dinamo Font Browser windows framed like classic desktop write tools, scaling from dense character strings up to display capitals with Are.naâs double-asterisk glyph tucked into the title bars and punctuation rows.

The revival doesnât stop at tidying up old curves. Dinamoâs wireframe designspace cube maps ABC Arealâs typography across three axes: Weight, Slant, and Proportion, stretching the character set smoothly from proportional spacing into monospaced territory. On the family overview sheet, that structure expands into eighteen cuts split across ABC Areal, ABC Areal Semi-Mono, and ABC Areal Mono, each carrying Regular, Medium, and Bold weights alongside matching italics. A clean three-circle Venn diagram sums up the commission without a slogan, placing Are.na, Dinamo, and Arial around Areal in the center. Itâs a working set of everyday typography built for dense research blocks, quiet headings, and anyone who wants a sharper, free alternative to the webâs oldest default.

‘I want the experiences I had to be available forever’: arts figures and scientists hit out at proposed job cuts at Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, more than 100 prominent figures across arts, politics and the media have published a joint letter criticising proposed job cuts at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG), Australia’s second oldest institution.
  • It has been revealed that TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium.
  • Highlights of the TMAG collection include a rare taxidermied Thylacine, colonial-era art, objects and more than 12,000 Tasmanian Aboriginal cultural artefacts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, more than 100 prominent figures across arts, politics and the media have published a joint letter criticising proposed job cuts at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG), Australia’s second oldest institution. The signatories include the former Tasmanian premier Lara Giddings and the 2014 Man Booker Prize winner Richard Flanagan, along with 44 leading-scientists representing universities in the UK, Europe, Canada, USA, Russia and Australia.

It has been revealed that TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium. Its “science collections are really critical on a global scale for research around climate change and species extinction,” explains Ian Terry, the chair of Friends of TMAG and the museum’s former senior curator of cultural heritage (2006-2017).

Highlights of the TMAG collection include a rare taxidermied Thylacine, colonial-era art, objects and more than 12,000 Tasmanian Aboriginal cultural artefacts.

Recent findings suggest that staff at the TMAG were briefed in August that up to 19.7 full time equivalent (FTE) jobs, or roughly 30% of its workforce would be axed to rein in government spending. The government has disputed the claim that the scale of the required cuts has been confirmed; a spokesperson is quoted in ABC News as saying “TMAG is not required to reduce its workforce by 30%”.

However, since news of cuts were made public Tasmanian MPs, TMAG’s executive and its board have received more than 25 letters from prominent European scientists that have decried the government’s planned cuts, and warned its decision to axe the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium, Gintaras Kantvilas, an internationally renowned biologist, would have “consequences far beyond Tasmania”.

This week’s letter called for the Tasmanian government to recognise its “statutory obligation to care for approximately one million objects of inestimable value” and “reconsider the proposed job cuts with their unintended deleterious consequences on the Tasmanian economy.”.

“I want TMAG properly funded. I want the life-changing childhood experiences I had at TMAG to be available to all Tasmanians forever,” David Walsh, the founder of Hobart’s Museum of Old and New Art (MONA), and one of the letter’s signatories, wrote in a separate letter that was published in Hobart’s Mercury newspaper this week. “I put stuff on Mona’s wall because TMAG put stuff in my heart,” he added.

The proposed job losses are part of wide-ranging cost cutting initiatives being rolled out by the state Liberal government, as part of an attempt to rein in the state’s ballooning debt, which is projected to reach A$9.9bn (£5bn) by 2027-28. These initiatives include a initiative to slash up 1700 public sector jobs by 2032.

Although the government disputes the scale of the proposed staff reductions, when a upcoming organisational chart was shown to staff in late September it identified “seven positions that were definitely to be cut,” Terry indicates. Those positions included two positions at the herbarium, a biologist, a graphic designer, a photographer, the museum’s only exhibitions officer, as well as the amalgamation of the vertebrate and invertebrate zoologist into a single role.

Asked about the government’s dismissal of the claims about a higher number of staff losing their jobs, Terry explains that over the last 12 months the museum has already lost “quite a lot of staff” through natural attrition and redundancies. “I suspect some of those positions were included in the 19.7 figure,” he notes.

TMAG and the Tasmania state premier’s department has been approached for comment by The Art Newspaper.

According to recent reports, according to independent budget analysis provided by the Friends of TMAG, the proposed changes under the broader cost-cutting initiative would also see TMAG move under the control of a upcoming government agency called Building Tasmania and lose up to 27% of its funding for 2027-28 while its targets for physical visitation increase by 6.4%. TMAG is already “seriously underfunded”, claims Terry. Its current exhibition Becoming Modern: Mid-century Australian Art has a 16-month run. “That's unheard of,” Terry continues, adding he thinks that “locals will be going less often because you're not going to go back many times to look at the same exhibition”.

In a recent development, A state government spokesperson says there is no correlation between the cost cutting measures and a newly introduced A$1.13bn (£573m) football stadium planned for Macquarie Point, a location that was once earmarked for a truth-and-reconciliation art park proposed by Dark Lab (a subsidiary of MONA). However, the independent MP Peter George asked in a statement issued on 25 September: “where’s the money [for that stadium] coming from?”.

The proposed cuts to staff numbers are right now under review by the Tasmanian Industrial Commission and Tasmania’s Upper House is voting on calls to reverse cuts to TMAG’s budget. Decisions on both complications are expected on Tuesday 24 November.

At the time of writing both Gintaras Kantvilas, the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium and Simon Grove, a zoologist and curator of invertebrates, have remarked they have had their positions reinstated after they had been under threat due to the proposed cuts.

Domes depict constellations of missiles in the night sky at Sharjah Architecture Triennial

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee have created three domed structures that reimagine constellations by mapping military objects in the night sky, which were displayed at this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.
  • Titled After Night There is Nothing, the trio of installations aim to bring attention to how communities are responding to drones, satellites, rockets and missiles changing the sky above them.
  • Covered in thatch, the three curved wood-and-steel structures are segments of a giant globe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee have created three domed structures that reimagine constellations by mapping military objects in the night sky, which were displayed at this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Titled After Night There is Nothing, the trio of installations aim to bring attention to how communities are responding to drones, satellites, rockets and missiles changing the sky above them.

Covered in thatch, the three curved wood-and-steel structures are segments of a giant globe.

Vinyl lines the inner curves, where Nahleh and Saloojee designed creature-like constellations based on man-made military objects in the sky.

The trio of installations were displayed at three venues at the Sharjah Architecture Triennial – the Al Qasimiyah School, a former slaughterhouse, and in the sandy Al Madam town.

It has been revealed that “This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” Nahleh told Dezeen. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”.

“The drones, missiles, rockets and satellites eclipse some of the constellations, and sometimes fuse with them,” he continued.

“That fusion is at the heart of this project – how do these technologies, through cultural practices on the ground, begin to morph into latest creatures and new constellations that people try to make sense of to interpret the violence of this military technology that is taking place.”.

Nahleh and Saloojee aimed to combine the reality of modern war with mythical storytelling, drawing upon their research into communities exposed to military attacks.

“We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing newly introduced mythical creatures – creatures that fuse together technological advancement with epistemic practices and myth-making practices that happen from the ground,” noted Nahleh.

“Most of these creatures, these modern constellations as we’re calling them, are populating the night sky in our drawing alongside pathways of flights of drones, satellites and other things that manifest across the night sky we’ve inherited, rather than the one we lost,” he continued.

“We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us, be it in the shape of missiles, phosphorus, or flares.”.

As well as depicting creature-like constellations in their inner curves, the structures themselves were designed as creatures – the nocturnal Solifugi spider known to run out the sun and into shade.

Sources indicate that “The project is dedicated to the Solifugi, which is a spider that by nature runs away from the sun, the sun of imperial savagery,” said Nahleh. “It has a very thick skin to protect it from this brightness, and in its belly is a map of the contemporary sky.”.

Three openings puncture the shell in each of the installations. In the desert site at Al Madam, a vertical cut-out frames a view of the minaret of a distant mosque, and at the slaughterhouse site, a long opening was set at the height of a cow.

Traditional Hakawati storytellers will narrate stories at the installations as part of the triennial, which runs until April.

“The story is difficult, but it’s about finding optimism,” mentioned Nahleh. “People are carving their own histories on the weapons that are here to annihilate them.”.

According to recent reports, “There’s a paradox here that we have to confront,” he continued. “When libraries are being erased, and people have no more books to publish or things to write on, they’re writing on the weapons that are sent to devour them.”.

Industry observers note that “Kids now are finding ways again to dream by placing their wishes upon the shooting stars, which are usually missiles and rockets. It’s a sad and complicated story, but we can no longer escape it by wishing for a sky we no longer have.”.

We rounded up eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which includes a draping shelter that pays homage to the improvised learning spaces created by Virginia’s Black community, and a circular canopy with cut-outs that plot 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun.

Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

Mondaine turns solar technology into design feature with Doppio Solar Skeleton timepiece

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Swiss watchmaker Mondaine has expanded its Doppio collection with the Solar Skeleton, a timepiece that brings solar technology into the foreground of its design.
  • Rather than concealing the solar plates beneath the dial, the watch reveals them through a precisely cut circular opening, turning a functional component into a defining visual feature.
  • The design builds on the distinctive visual language of Mondaine‘s Doppio collection, which is characterised by double-line hands and indexes, a concave dial and a double-domed sapphire crystal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swiss watchmaker Mondaine has expanded its Doppio collection with the Solar Skeleton, a timepiece that brings solar technology into the foreground of its design.

Rather than concealing the solar plates beneath the dial, the watch reveals them through a precisely cut circular opening, turning a functional component into a defining visual feature.

The design builds on the distinctive visual language of Mondaine‘s Doppio collection, which is characterised by double-line hands and indexes, a concave dial and a double-domed sapphire crystal.

Mondaine explained that these elements establish a sense of repetition, rhythm and structural clarity, while the exposed solar plates introduce an additional layer of depth and visual interest.

While solar technology is typically hidden from view, Mondaine has taken a different approach with the Doppio Solar Skeleton.

A carefully positioned circular opening around the centre of the dial offers a controlled view of the solar movement, while the outer section retains the indexes to ensure clear readability.

By making the technology visible, Mondaine aimed to bridge the watch’s technical function with its aesthetic identity, without compromising the “clarity and legibility” that define the collection.

Powered by a Swiss Ronda solar movement, the watch converts natural and artificial light into electrical energy, which is stored in a rechargeable battery.

According to Mondaine, a few minutes of sunlight can reactivate a fully discharged movement, while a full charge provides a power reserve of up to eight months in complete darkness.

The brand explained that this technology eliminates the need for regular battery replacements, offering a more resource-conscious approach to timekeeping.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton is available in two versions, each offering a different interpretation of its distinctive design.

The first combines a polished silver 316L stainless steel case with a vegan grape leather strap, bringing together traditional watchmaking materials and a contemporary material alternative.

The second features a polished black stainless steel case paired with a matching mesh bracelet, creating a more monochromatic appearance that emphasises the watch’s clean lines and geometric detailing.

Both versions feature a 41-millimetre case, a discreet date window and a precisely laser-etched Mondaine logo and solar markings.

A double-domed sapphire crystal and water resistance of up to 5 ATM complete the design, “combining refined aesthetics with everyday practicality”.

“With the Doppio Solar Skeleton, we wanted to make solar technology part of the design itself,” said Mondaine.

“By revealing the cells beneath the dial, we have created a watch where functionality becomes a defining aesthetic feature, while staying true to Mondaine’s principles of clarity, precision and Swiss design.”.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton reflects Mondaine’s commitment to iconic Swiss minimalist design, where form and function work together.

By integrating visible solar technology into the collection’s established design language, the watch intends to demonstrate how a functional element can become an integral part of a timepiece’s aesthetic identity.

To find out more about Mondaine and the Doppio Solar Skeleton, visit the brand’s website.

Efforts to save I.M. Pei’s Dallas City Hall likely headed to referendum

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when the mayor of Dallas, Erik Jonsson, inaugurated I.M.
  • Since early 2025, the current Dallas mayor Eric Johnson and city manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert have pushed to abandon and sell Pei’s city hall to private developers.
  • Recent findings suggest that in recent interviews, Johnson has sounded far different from his predecessor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when the mayor of Dallas, Erik Jonsson, inaugurated I.M. Pei’s city hall in 1978, he called it “a monument to the city’s pride, a symbol of a first-class city that’s reaching for greatness”. The seven-storey inverted pyramid slopes over a large plaza with site-specific sculptures like Henry Moore’s Vertebra in Three Pieces (1978, also known as The Dallas Piece) and Marta Pan’s Floating Sculpture (1973), which sits in a reflecting pool.

Since early 2025, the current Dallas mayor Eric Johnson and city manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert have pushed to abandon and sell Pei’s city hall to private developers. They have cited the prohibitive costs of renovating the building, which ballooned within a matter of months from $81m according to an initial estimate for a basic infrastructure upgrade to $1.4bn for massive upgrades over two decades.

Recent findings suggest that in recent interviews, Johnson has sounded far different from his predecessor. He has called the building “obsolete”. Architecturally significant or not, moving the municipal headquarters “would make this location available for development, which I would also support. I believe that will be a very, very significant part of the future of downtown and its revitalisation.” Spokespersons for the city did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s questions.

The current mayor is in alignment with the “Say Yes to Downtown” campaign group led by former mayor Mike Rawlings. With developers and other former leaders, the campaign argues that city hall must be demolished to create an entertainment district, including a newly introduced arena for two of the city’s professional sports teams, the Dallas Mavericks basketball team and the Stars hockey team. When the teams revealed intends to move out of the city’s core, both considered relocating to the city hall site. They ultimately chose other locations.

Amid the uproar over the possible demolition of Pei’s modernist complex, few have questioned the fate of Pan’s and Moore’s sculptures. Both were gifted to the city and are part of the municipal public art collection. But the future of Moore’s, which has required previous renovation, in part with help from the artist’s London-based estate and foundation, is a particular concern. The large grouping of organic forms was meant to complement Pei’s rigidly angular structure. It was also a gift to the city from the philanthropist W.R. Hawn in memory of his wife Mildred Hawn, whose favourite sculptor was Moore. Both sculptures are part of the preservation blueprint for the building; representatives for Moore and Pan’s estates did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries.

Dallas City Hall The Lyda Hill Texas Collection of Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith's America Project, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

According to recent reports, the non-profit Save Dallas City Hall, an ideologically diverse grassroots coalition, has been among the loudest voices opposed to moving the facility. It is led by president Bruce Richardson, a musician, artist and former political candidate, and vice-president Zaida Basora, an architect and former city employee who oversaw maintenance of properties, including city hall, and at the moment serves as the executive director of the American Institute of Architects Dallas.

Basora and her colleagues have proposed a ten-year phased strategy that, even factoring in inflation, is estimated to cost between $70m and $100m, and would not require municipal staff to move. The cost of simply demolishing the building—to say nothing of the expense of building something in its place—has been estimated at $60m.

The Dallas city council gave Tolbert a deadline of 26 August to present relocation options for city hall, which she missed. Inflation has also increased the cost of relocating. The same month, Save Dallas City Hall sued the city, arguing that it was committing “demolition by neglect”.

Recent findings suggest that “Dallas city hall has at least one failed generator, active parking garage leaks and is due for roof maintenance,” Richardson said in a statement. “Instead of tackling these problems with millions in available funds, the city halted repairs, wasting money and time to explore a move.”.

In a recent development, on 2 October, the Save Dallas City Hall coalition started an effort to gather signatures to create a ballot referendum on the fate of city hall, which would be put to residents for a vote in May 2027. In early November, the group declared it had gathered around 25,000 signatures—well over the minimum 20,000 signatures needed for a ballot referendum. If the group’s proposed amendment to the city charter passes next spring, the municipal government will be required to continue operating from Pei’s city hall.

During elections earlier this month, 56% of Dallas voters opposed a $443m bond package. That package had included funding to move emergency operations out of city hall, which, according to advocates of preserving Pei’s building, would have been a first step toward abandoning it.

For the local activist Stephanie Drenka, a co-founder of the Dallas Asian American Historical Society who has spoken at nearly every public hearing since she learned of the building’s significance, preserving city hall is essential to recognising Pei’s contribution to Asian American history.

“The stakes are beyond our city alone,” she indicates. Less than 1% of historic markers in the US acknowledge the contributions of Asian Americans, according to the national non-profit Asian & Pacific Islander Americans in Historic Preservation.

Sources indicate that “This also makes demolition of city hall an issue of further erasure of Asian Americans in history,” Drenka says. “It’s not just Pei’s legacy, but we’re defending ourselves. Everything in our community is embodied in this building.” She adds: “If we can’t save city hall then what threat can we stop?”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Base Design rebuilds The Huntington brand identity around a sculpted H monogram, a hidden gem idea and green drawn from pigment and plant life.
  • It has been revealed that the Huntington is a library, an art museum and botanical gardens on 200 acres in Southern California, founded in 1919, and most visitors knew only the gardens.
  • The wordmark is set in a serif with flared terminals, THE HUNTINGTON debossed into a green textured surface so the letters read as much by shadow as by ink.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Base Design rebuilds The Huntington brand identity around a sculpted H monogram, a hidden gem idea and green drawn from pigment and plant life.

It has been revealed that the Huntington is a library, an art museum and botanical gardens on 200 acres in Southern California, founded in 1919, and most visitors knew only the gardens. Base Design starts from the mark itself. Two flanking pillars in lime green hold a diamond shaped gem at the center, set against a deep green field. The studio calls the idea a hidden gem, treasured, layered, quietly extraordinary, and the mark behaves that way. It never shouts. It sits still and lets the green do the talking, while accents shift like light on a leaf or oil on canvas.

The wordmark is set in a serif with flared terminals, THE HUNTINGTON debossed into a green textured surface so the letters read as much by shadow as by ink. The same voice carries the exhibition posters, where single words stack large and flat. ROSE breaks across four stacked lines in pink, cut-out rose photographs tucked between the letters, on a poster lying in the flower beds. The orchid show poster sets its title in pink and purple over a full-bleed orchid photograph.

According to recent reports, the H doubles as a pattern. On the What's On board it repeats in four colourways, orange, green, blue and yellow, each stem holding its gem. A close crop of the mark fills a whole frame with one lime stem and crossbar against dark green, the curve of the pillar edge doing all the work.

According to recent reports, print carries the system. Brochures rest on giant green leaves, their covers carrying the H and the names of the collections. A flat lay of the print suite shows the orchid show poster, the bonsai collection guide, a portrait exhibition guide and a yellow Stories from the Library sheet, each piece holding the same green and the same serif. The Library Quarterly sits on a leather chair, its cream cover and red masthead quiet against the dark wood around it.

Industry observers note that outside, the system scales up without changing its voice. A dark green wayfinding totem stands among the planting, its directory set in small capitals above the H at the base.

Two exhibition billboards pair portraits with green type, one for Mineo Mizuno, one for Don Bachardy, and the same green runs through the noticeboards.

See more from Base Design on their website.
