After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that during my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal.
  • Recent findings suggest that at the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy.
  • If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that during my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal. It was sharp, persistent, and unsettling in a way I couldn’t ignore. As a former labor and delivery nurse, I understood the risks in a way many patients do not. I knew what to watch for. I knew my history. I knew when something felt wrong. Yet when I raised concerns, they were not met with the urgency they deserved.

Recent findings suggest that at the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy. I knew that the vertical incision on my uterus could put a future pregnancy at risk. I spoke up. I asked questions. I paid attention to my body. Still, when I experienced a uterine rupture, I was navigating a system that did not respond with the level of care and urgency that the moment required.

If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?

In a recent development, conversations during Black Maternal Health Week often center around one urgent truth: Black women are still far more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes in this country than white women. This is not an assumption. It is a proven fact, and it should stop all of us in our tracks. It also does not only impact one socioeconomic group. It affects everyone, including some of the most visible and resourced women in the world.

Recent findings suggest that as the founder of Mielle, my mission is to empower women, especially Black women, to express their authentic selves. At its core, that mission is about care, agency, and visibility, which is why conversations like this matter. It’s about showing up for every part of Black women’s experience. We need to talk more candidly about what happens to Black women who survive the trauma of miscarriage or stillbirth, and the prolonged mental health challenges that can follow, including postpartum depression.

Black women are expected to remain “strong” while navigating medical emergencies. We’re dismissed, told to wait, to calm down, and to trust a system that has not always earned that trust. We survive experiences that change our families and us forever. And then, too often, we are expected to do something just as impossible: keep going as if survival is the end of the story. It is not.

That is why Black Maternal Health Week cannot be about mortality alone. It must also be about what it means to live after trauma, preventable harm, and loss that reshapes your life.

It has been revealed that the data make clear that this crisis is ongoing. Black women are about three times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes than white women, and more than 80% of those deaths are considered preventable. Black infants also die at more than twice the rate of white infants. These are not random gaps. They reflect a healthcare system and a culture that too often normalizes Black women’s pain instead of responding to it.

Industry observers note that research highlights that one in five women, or about 20%, report mistreatment during maternity care, but for Black women, that figure climbs to nearly 30%, reflecting more frequent experiences of bias, disrespect, and lack of autonomy in clinical settings. Nearly half of women say they have held back from asking questions or sharing concerns. In one of the most vulnerable moments of a person’s life, too many are already calculating whether speaking up will make things worse.

Industry observers note that in my own life, grief did not arrive quietly. It entered my marriage, my motherhood, my body, my faith, and eventually my work. In my book, The Glory In Your Story, I write about how grief does not follow a timeline. It becomes part of who you are, and healing begins not by outrunning it, but by acknowledging it.

In a recent development, that matters because so many Black women are praised for being strong when what we actually need is space to be human. After losing Milan, I returned to work. I kept moving. I built Mielle. From the outside, it can look like a story of resilience. And in many ways, it is. But we have to be honest about the lessons we take from stories like mine.

The lesson should not be that Black women are uniquely equipped to carry devastating grief and still perform at a high level. It should not be that our resilience makes systemic failures acceptable. And it should not be that we have to turn survival into something productive just to make our pain legible.

Too often, we celebrate the comeback without sitting long enough with the conditions that made it necessary.

Faith carried me. Purpose helped me rebuild. But none of that changes the reality that more listening, better care, stronger hospital systems, and greater urgency might have changed my story. If we are serious about maternal health, we have to be just as serious about saying that clearly.

According to recent reports, black Maternal Health Week gives us an opportunity to think more broadly about what justice looks like. It looks like hospitals are equipped for emergencies. It looks like providers who listen to Black women the first time, without requiring patients to fight to be believed. It looks like support for families after loss–not just during a crisis. And it looks like making space for grief without expecting Black women to turn it into inspiration before we are ready.

It’s time that we honor not only the women we have lost, but also the women still here carrying what the system could not or would not hold for them. Survival is not the finish line. Being heard, protected, and cared for should be.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that paris-based foundry Production Type has revived the classic French typeface Vendôme, restoring it to its former glory.
  • Industry observers note that in its early days, Vendôme was one of the best serif fonts – a celebration of France's post-WWII creative boom.
  • Vendôme first made its debut back in 1950, drawn by sculptor and set designer François Ganeau, with meticulous art direction from Roger Excoffon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that paris-based foundry Production Type has revived the classic French typeface Vendôme, restoring it to its former glory. Once tainted by poor handwritten recreations and clunky scans, the font eventually lost its lustre, but with patience and craft, Production Type has revitalised this classic for the better.

Industry observers note that in its early days, Vendôme was one of the best serif fonts – a celebration of France's post-WWII creative boom. Making a playful, contemporary debut, the latest Vendôme Nouveau is a love letter to French heritage, with a elegant, modern refinement.

Vendôme first made its debut back in 1950, drawn by sculptor and set designer François Ganeau, with meticulous art direction from Roger Excoffon. Defined by its "leaning stems, wavering strokes, plunging Vs, and abruptly sharp serifs," the typeface became an icon of design, featuring on ads, book jackets, record sleeves, and film posters.

But the legendary font soon began to suffer from its own success, being recreated by sign painters and shopkeepers who wanted a slice of its fame. With the rise of phototypesetting, the font was endlessly copied, and by the 90s, the iconic typeface had countless iterations with varying degrees of quality and style.

Recent findings suggest that refusing to let the icon die, the Production Type team (and type historian PhDs) set about restoring the font to its former glory. A labour of love, the process took over 20 years of meticulous redrawing, using an array of archival paper proofs and filling the gaps of missing weights from scratch.

The font made an unconventional and wonderfully contemporary debut on the NYC subway, where commuters were snapped reading fake typographic self-help books like “How to Raise a Sans Serif in an All-Serif Family”.

Discover more about the project or take a look at the most iconic typefaces ever made.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that two person shows are taking over the art world, with galleries doubling as matchmakers, mostly pairing dead artists with market darlings. But of course, nothing beats conversation between two old friends.

At Gladstone in Newly introduced York this fall, that’s just what you’ll get, with a new show from British artists Sarah Lucas and Cerith Wyn Evans titled “Je Pense.”.

Recent findings suggest that the two talked to Art in America about the exhibition, and their 30-year friendship, below. Related Articles Julia Stoschek Collection to Celebrate 20 Years with 'Selfish in Bed' Exhibition and Düsseldorf Reopening Sarah Lucas Wins New Museum's $400,000 Sculpture Prize.

Recent findings suggest that you two have been friends since the ’90s. How’d you meet?

Cerith Wyn Evans: I never can answer questions like that because I never remember. We were probably both drunk somewhere.

CWE: I do remember hearing of you. I was close with a painter at the time, Angus Cook, and I’d ask him things like “What’s Gary Hume like?,” all this kind of stuff. Later I quipped, “We should really be talking about his girlfriend, a much better artist. She’s called Sarah Lucas.”.

Angus said he had met you once: He knocked on the door and you answered—allegedly!—and he said “Hi, are you Gary?” and you replied “NO.” He told me “Oh my God, She’s incredible!”.

In a recent development, SL: I remember meeting Angus at a party Matthew Marks gave for Gary, maybe that’s where I met you. A lot of things were happening at that time, around 1990; something was burgeoning. I met a lot of people then that became friends for life.

You can’t make newly introduced old friends! When I saw that you two were showing together, I admit my first thought was: a minimalist and a maximalist walk into a bar.

According to recent reports, CWE: Who’s who? [laughs] I’m certainly the maximalist.

Recent findings suggest that ha. All that’s to say, at first glance, I thought of you two as having quite different sensibilities, but they really do converge beautifully in the gallery. I know you’ve wanted to show together for quite a while.

SL: We’ve kicked the notion around for a long time, but it was more of a mythic show, something we might do some day—it wasn’t about whether we ever did it or not.

Industry observers note that CWE: I think if you really really care how another person thinks, if you don’t take them for granted, you imagine your dialogue… but also the distance between our work allows a certain level of respect. Nancy Spector invited us, and really, the show’s a kind of hologram that Nancy has somehow… well, she’s the Wizard of Oz.

Recent findings suggest that so the differences help. Okay, I have to ask about the burnt-out car in the gallery, obviously.

CWE: For me, that’s the fulcrum of the entire exhibition because it’s so brutal. It’s like a black hole in the middle of the entire thing, and a vortex that everything sucks everything else in, or spits it all out, or something. It’s phenomenal, extraordinary and also this quotidian tragedy, a very pure readymade. Sarah bought it at an auction, already burnt. I guess weird death perverts buy these things.

SL: I have no idea who would buy these things… apart from us.

Did you make the work in tandem and blueprint it out, or just bring things together at the end? I love how Sarah’s sculpture makes Cerith’s tower feel very phallic.

CWE: No, we’ve just always been very erotic, very horny. See, this is the maximalist in me coming out.

SL: Besides, things are always different when you get them somewhere anyway.

Have you guys been like doing studio visits and giving each other feedback over the years?

Recent findings suggest that CWE: No no no. It’s organic. It’s natural. It’s spiritual. We’re not really that organized.

SL: That’s probably why we like each other. We get on because we don’t have that kind of mindset that would make us, I don’t know, strategic.

I’m just thinking about a lot of younger artists who are working hard to sustain creative community. I don’t know if you have thoughts or advice for them.

SL: No one takes advice, do they? Though I will say, younger artists should be in more group shows. When you’re young, you’re so eager to have your moment in the spotlight.

Has your friendship ever felt competitive?

According to recent reports, SL: We just aren’t really strategic like that. I’m not a jealous person by nature. I’m just in my own world, making work.

CWE: I think it’s sad when people compare themselves and are concerned with who’s more famous or younger or richer.

Do you talk about art together then, or other stuff?

In a recent development, CWE: I don’t think I talk about anything else. But it depends what how you by mean “Art.” I’m obsessed by creativity more than much art with a price tag.

SL: That’s true, art can be anything.

#194528. Tech Report: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

Tech Report: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on.
  • It has been revealed that if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone.
  • There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

It has been revealed that if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

Industry observers note that “The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”.

Although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

According to recent reports, sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, states Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

According to recent reports, the textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

Some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

All things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin indicates. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

It has been revealed that regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin says.

Because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin claims. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

Industry observers note that women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, states Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

Recent findings suggest that and it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin notes. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

It has been revealed that home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin claims. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”.

According to recent reports, that’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health problems.

Recent findings suggest that if left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, notes Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really promptly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

Over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra indicates, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

In a recent development, because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition challenges and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar states. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research highlights that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

As researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s crucial to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A touchscreen MacBook has been on the wishlist of many Mac consumers (and media commentators) for years, and now it’s finally here. While Apple hasn’t gone all the way and produced a 2-in-1 MacBook with a stylus, there are some applications for the touchscreen tech in creative apps, and the switch to OLED means there's incredible brightness on offer. The massive drawback is that it’s even more expensive, especially as it only comes on top-end machines, but one day every MacBook might be like this.

Expensive, expensive, expensive.

Force Touch trackpad not immediately intuitive.

Sources indicate that why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

There's a lot of ‘pro’ in this laptop. It’s a MacBook Pro. It has an M5 Pro CPU inside it. And it has Apple’s fresh PROLED XDR screen, which is a touchscreen OLED to everyone else. Is there any way that more pro-ness could have been squeezed in? Perhaps one of the Radeon Pro GPUs that graced the ‘Darth Vader’s dustbin’ generation of the Mac Pro?

Sources indicate that that aside, we might be looking at the future of the MacBook line. While for now the new screen is only available on a few top-end models, the benefits it brings - not only improved brightness but a thinner and lighter chassis - are likely to trickle down through the range.

According to recent reports, the MacBook Pro remains pro-fessional, has a powerful pro-cessor, and Apple’s hardware pro-wess means we shouldn’t get any pro-blems from the PROLED display. Let’s see. It could be heading to the top of our best laptop for animation guide.

3x Thunderbolt 5, 1x HDMI 2.1, 3.5mm audio.

• Slightly slimmer than before• Not a 2-in-1.

Industry observers note that first things first, the PROLED screen makes the 16in MacBook Pro a little slimmer and lighter. It’s also a stunner in terms of colour and brightness, but Apple is so late to this party it’s a little hard to get overexcited. We’ve had OLED touchscreens on Windows PCs since at least 2016 and Lenovo’s Yoga 14, and while the display tech is magnificent it does mean you end up with fingermarks all over your screen, especially if you’re using it after lunch.

Industry observers note that then there's the debate about what touchscreen laptops are actually for. In 2-in-1 designs you can bend the screen back and whip out a stylus for some sketching, but in a traditional laptop you’re more likely to use it for zooming and scrolling. Apple’s announcement event for the laptop showed someone using the touchscreen to play piano keys directly on its screen, and while this somehow seems unlikely, as surely your hands will be in entirely the wrong position, it can also be used to click and drag files, audio tracks, and to do a little precision brushwork with your fingertip if you need to. Happily, it’s optional, and the MacBook trackpad is as good as ever. The touchscreen supports most trackpad gestures, if you’re the sort to let their fingers dance, and as ever you can pay extra for the Nanotexture coating that cuts reflections.

In a recent development, elsewhere, you get the usual MacBook Pro build. They’re really well made, and this one’s no exception. The switch to OLED has allowed for a millimetre to be shaved off the laptop’s thickness, and a few hundred grams to be shed from its weight. The weight reduction is the more noticeable of the two, making Apple’s largest laptop a touch more portable. By far the most notable thing, however, is that the Apple logo on the MacBook’s lid once again lights up when the laptop is in use, and it’s the right way up.

• Thunderbolt 5• Excellent colour reproduction.

There are three Thunderbolt 5 ports on the MacBook Pro 16, all of which are compatible with USB4 peripherals, and as there's a full-size HDMI 2.1 port and a MagSafe 3 for charging, you won’t have to bog them down connecting to monitors and chargers. This opens them up for use with external SSDs, and given the extra cost of upgrading the storage in a modern Mac when you order, one of those will probably be on your shopping list.

In a recent development, the screen is the significant latest feature for this 2026 release of the MacBook Pro 16, and this new OLED is an absolute beauty. It’s a ‘tandem’ OLED, which stacks two light-emitting layers on top of one another for a brightness boost, and it reveals: Apple promises up to 2,000 nits of brightness if you feed it HDR content, a figure that rivals even its immensely bright Studio Display XDR. Colour is excellent too though you’ll need to manually activate the PROLED XDR P3 + AdobeRGB colour profile in the Settings app to get the most out of it. Do this, and you can expect 93% of Adobe RGB and 94% of DCI-P3 alongside 100% of sRGB.

Apple has also fiddled with the MacBook Pro’s hinge for a better touchscreen experience. Push too hard and you can find a laptop’s screen leaning away from you, but the hinge on the PROLED is noticeably stiffer than that on a non-touch MacBook. It’s also incredibly smooth, almost like there's some sort of hydraulic aspect to it, as it moves up and down.

It has been revealed that on the front you’ll find Apple’s usual keyboard, which is pretty good, and a Force Touch trackpad that can take a bit of getting used to, especially if you’re used to holding the pad in to drag files about. This can trigger a deeper click that brings up file information, which is less useful than you might think, but it doesn’t take long to get the hang of, and you can change what it does in the settings.

We test every one of our laptops using the same benchmarking software suite to give you a thorough overview of its suitability for creatives of all disciplines and levels. This includes:.

• Geekbench: Tests the CPU for single-core and multi-core power, and the GPU for the system's potential for gaming, image processing, or video editing. Geekbench AI tests the CPU and GPU on a variety of AI-powered and AI-boosted tasks.• Cinebench: Tests the CPU and GPU's ability to run Cinema 4D and Redshift.• UL Procyon: Uses UL Solutions' Procyon software suite to test the system's ability for AI image generation in Stable Diffusion, its Microsoft Office performance and its battery life in a looping video test.• Topaz Video AI: We use Topaz Video AI to test the system's ability to upscale video and convert video to slow-motion.• PugetBench for Creators: We use the PugetBench for Creators benchmarking suite to test the system's ability to run several key tasks in Photoshop and Adobe Premiere Pro, as well as its performance when encoding/transcoding video.• ON1 Resize AI: Tests the system's ability to resize 5 photos to 200% in a batch process. We take the total time taken to resize the images and divide by 5.

• Very fast CPU• GPU can't beat descrete chips.

The PROLED MacBook is a premium product, and so comes with a choice of premium processors (and a premium price, but more on that later). It can be fitted with an M5 Pro, which is what we’ve got here, or an M5 Max that piles on the processing cores. There's no option for anything else, so you won’t be picking one up with a vanilla M5 in it. The M5 Pro and Max both use Apple’s Fusion Architecture to weld CPU dies together into one mega-chip, and the core counts make it look very much like the Pro is two normal M5s stuck together, with two cores disabled. It’s split into six Super cores and 12 Performance cores - the old Efficient cores are missing from this generation - and it can turbo up to 4.6 GHz.

Apple’s claim that the M5 offers the fastest single-core performance out there remains unbeaten in our tests. In the Geekbench 6 single-core test, the M5 Pro comes within a hair’s breadth of the M5 Max in a Mac Studio, a remarkable feat for a laptop. The Studio pulls ahead a bit in the multi-core test due to having more cores, but the Pro is right up there, actually beating the M5 Max from when we tested it in a MacBook Pro and leaving the M4 Pro behind.

Recent findings suggest that the fastest non-Apple single-core result in our tests, the Asus Zenbook A16 powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Elite, now rests in tenth place in the Geekbench charts, and you have to go to 13th place before you find an X86 CPU, which is in a desktop gaming PC. Apple is completely dominant in this arena at the moment, and it’s only when you switch to the GPU test results that the gaming PCs rise to the top and the Apple chips get some real competition.

In real-world applications, the M5 Pro isn’t as fast at doing tasks such as denoising raw files in Adobe Camera Raw as an Nvidia GPU, but it’s way faster than trying to do it using the integrated graphics on most Intel or AMD chips.

Sources indicate that the battery life of all the M5 generation MacBooks has been exceptional, but the OLED screen has tipped the 16in Pro over the edge into a machine that can be relied on for two whole days of use. Testing how long it could play a video until exhausted took a lot longer than on most other laptops, with a final figure in excess of 21 hours. Push it really hard and that will come down, of course, but it’s a remarkable achievement nonetheless.

This is the thing that’s going to keep these first touchscreen Macs out of the hands of many creatives. The 16in model we’ve got here starts at £3,399 for one with 24GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, and just climbs and climbs as you add more stuff to it. You want 64GB of RAM and 4TB of storage? You can have it, but it’ll cost you £5,899 and you can go higher than that if you switch to the M5 Max. The touchscreen is a premium feature, and the same laptop with the old display starts from £2,999. The old M5 model no longer seems to be available, probably to make way for an M6, which is already there on the 14in version.

Recent findings suggest that the fact this laptop even exists means Apple thinks there's a market for it, and if you’re a touchscreen laptop lover it may be the machine you’ve been dreaming of. There's no denying the expense, however, which means you’re really going to have to love it to consider it over other, better-value, choices.

Thinner and lighter than before.

Excellent CPU performance, GPU can't fight Nvidia.

Closer in performance to the MacBook Pro than to the MacBook Neo, the M5 edition of the MacBook Air is the bargain in Apple's range.

The frist generation of Nvidia's RTX Spark hardware looks promising for creatives. This 14-incher from Asus is powerful, well built, beautifully thin and light, and will last all day on a charge.

In a recent development, A mighty gaming laptop with a powerful GPU can make a good buy for a video editor or designer who likes to work on complex documents. This one from HP is slightly more subtly designed than many, and though its battery life is short it can surely speed up your workflows.

Ian Evenden has been a journalist for over 20 years, starting in the days of QuarkXpress 4 and Photoshop 5. He now mainly works in Creative Cloud and Google Docs, but can always find a use for a powerful laptop or two. When not sweating over page layout or photo editing, you can find him peering at the stars or growing vegetables.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in this quiet, 17th-century Parisian apartment on rue de Savoie in the 6th arrondissement, strange-looking insects appear to be climbing up the middle of the living room wall near the chimney. But these 15 or so critters—spiders, ants, and cockroaches—are actually drawn and carefully protected by glass coverings.

Industry observers note that that’s because they were made by none other than Pablo Picasso, once a regular visitor to this home, where his lover, the artist Dora Maar, lived from 1946 until she died in 1997. The abode, along with the Picasso drawings on the wall, is now for sale, listed for the lump sum of €2.85 million (about $3.1 million), reports Le Parisien. How’s that for a dinner party icebreaker? Related Articles Christie's Buzzy 20th-Century Sale Totals $626.6 M., with Starry Lots Above $80 M. by Kandinsky and Klimt Seven Works Reportedly from Jeff Koons's Collection Fetch a Lackluster $104 M. at Christie's, Led by a $31.2 M. Picasso.

Sources indicate that picasso used to call Maar “ma puce,” which literally means “my flea” and is used as an endearing term in French for “my sweetheart.” It is believed Picasso’s drawings were a playful pun on his nickname for Maar, per the apartment’s current owner, identified only as Ida. “They give it a history,” she added.

All the wall artworks have been officially recognized by the Picasso Administration, which manages the artist’s estate, and oversees a committee that catalogs his works.

It has been revealed that many may know Maar (1907–97) as the famous figure Picasso depicted in many paintings over the course of their seven-year relationship, including his “Weeping Woman” series, and another portrait of her from 1943 that sold for $37 million in 2025, quadrupling its estimate. Yet Maar herself has been belatedly recognized for her own paintings and photographs that contributed to the Surrealist movement’s heyday in Paris from the 1920s to the 1940s.

According to recent reports, the 1,600-square-foot apartment’s well-lit rooms, large windows, and high ceilings do fit an artistic sensibility, said the owner. With two bedrooms, an office, kitchen, and the famous Picasso-drawn living room, the Maar’s former home also boasts 13th-century petrified wooden beams from a former mansion that was converted into the apartment building.

Future owners of Maar’s apartment will also be able to hop over to the Louvre and the Centre Pompidou, right across the Seine River. Then again, if the urge to see art by a modern master strikes them, they won’t even need to leave their living room.

Grand Theft Auto VI takes over Miami, including its art destinations

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, a massive marketing campaign for the blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA) VI has transformed Miami—and the city’s art scene is coming along for the joyride.
  • On 13 October, the street art-focused Wynwood Walls museum unveiled a collaboration with the game’s developer Rockstar Games, inviting ten artists to create GTA-themed murals in and around the museum property.
  • According to recent reports, the art-centric campaign is part of a massive marketing push around the game, which was released globally on 19 November to universal critical acclaim.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, a massive marketing campaign for the blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA) VI has transformed Miami—and the city’s art scene is coming along for the joyride.

On 13 October, the street art-focused Wynwood Walls museum unveiled a collaboration with the game’s developer Rockstar Games, inviting ten artists to create GTA-themed murals in and around the museum property. The museum also confirmed the partnership would include merchandising and free admission for all Miami-Dade County residents until the end of 2028, reversing a pandemic-era policy that saw tickets sold at the attraction for the first time.

According to recent reports, the art-centric campaign is part of a massive marketing push around the game, which was released globally on 19 November to universal critical acclaim. Set in a satirical version of Miami called “Vice City”, the game world is an incredibly detailed virtual replica of the real city and the surrounding state of Florida (“Leonida”), complete with areas such as “Stockyard” replicating Wynwood with its street art and graffiti culture.

Art galleries in the digital replica of Wynwood (the "Stockyard" neighbourhood) inside Grand Theft Auto VI Screenshot by The Art Newspaper. Courtesy Rockstar Games.

Sources indicate that demonstrating an extreme dedication to realism, Rockstar has even painstakingly replicated and renamed local landmarks such as the nightclub Club Space (“The Vault”), the beloved regional casual dining chain Flanagan’s (“Uncle Jack’s) and local art institutions such as the Pérez Art Museum Miami ("Future Leonida Art Museum", or "Flam") and the Wolfsonian–Florida International University design museum ("Hicksonian Museum of Art and Design"). Miami Beach’s Bass Museum of Art (“Vice City Museum of Art”) had its iconic Ugo Rondinone sculpture Miami Mountain (2016) turned into a monumental stack of emojis inside the game. (Unfortunately the current exhibition at the "Vice City Museum of Art", Karl Bergstrom: Diaspora, cannot be visited as the building is not presently accessible within gameplay.).

Sources indicate that according to Jessica Goldman Srebnick, the Wynwood Walls museum’s chief executive and curator, Rockstar commissioned in-game murals from around 50 artists, many of whom have exhibited at the museum before. When the developer approached the museum to suggest a collaboration, it was a no-brainer. “Street art and gaming have a lot of shared cultural DNA, and they’ve influenced each other,” she notes. The game’s creators “share our commitment to creativity, to supporting artists. They share our commitment and deep appreciation for the city of Miami. And I’m just really grateful that they are supporting something that provides more access to the arts.”.

A Grand Theft Auto VI-themed mural by Queen Andrea in the real Wynwood neighbourhood of Miami Courtesy Queen Andrea and Wynwood Walls Museum.

The murals in Wynwood, which will be on display until 1 January 2027, are similar to those featured in the game itself. A mural by the artist Queen Andrea, for instance, reads “Welcome to Vice City” in a curvy, neon-like font, while another by Ron English features a design with grenades in the shape of lightbulbs and the slogan: “There’s nothing more dangerous than a good idea.”.

The project, as well as GTA’s larger presence in the city, has not been without controversy. The local newspaper Miami Latest Times reported on 10 November that one of the GTA murals had covered up a piece by the late artist Alex “Rect” Reyes, who finished the work shortly before his death in 2022. The wall had been considered a memorial by Reyes’s family and friends, who say they were not informed about its replacement. Goldman Global Arts, which owns the wall and museum, mentioned in a statement to the New Times that it had offered Reyes’s crew a different wall to make amends.

The digital replica of Miami Beach's Bass Museum of Art within Grand Theft Auto VI, the "Vice City Museum of Art", with an emoji-themed parody of its Ugo Rondinone public sculpture Image courtesy of IGN / Official Grand Theft Auto VI Strategy Guide.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, a joint partnership with Miami-Dade County and the Miami Heat professional basketball team has resulted in everything from player uniforms to the Kaseya Center arena in Downtown Miami being rebranded with “Vice City”. Massive crowds turned out for a Heat game on 18 November, the eve of the GTA VI’s release, to purchase custom merchandise that was only available at the arena. The total package, which includes lighting and signage inspired by the game at Miami International Airport and PortMiami, is valued at $3.9m according to a press release from the county government. Some officials have expressed alarm at the collaboration, with one county commissioner worried that the game is “depicting Miami like a murder capital”, according to the Miami Herald.

As for the benefits for the local art scene, perhaps gamers who visit GTA VI’s virtual “Vice City Museum of Art” will be inspired to seek out the Bass on their next visit to Miami Beach.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.
  • Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.
  • Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.

Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

Monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home’s original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G, was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for new inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

“The restoration was extremely respectful of the house’s original architecture, but we never wanted the result to feel nostalgic,” Gutiérrez told Dezeen.

“Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely newly introduced, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for.”.

Industry observers note that completed in February 2026, the design uses colour to achieve the transformation, bringing new energy to the original architecture without competing with it. The studio aimed to have the house be recognisably Mexican without falling into tropes.

“I wanted the house to feel unmistakably Mexican, but without relying on folklore or the usual clichés associated with ‘Mexican interiors’.” he mentioned.

“I was much more interested in expressing that identity through materials, craftsmanship, colour and contemporary Mexican design.”.

At the centre of the house, a dark-toned timber structure rises through a series of split levels like a sculptural tree connecting the entrance hall, living room, dining room, study and reading areas before unfolding into a double-height ceiling.

“More than a structural element, it serves as a spatial anchor, establishing continuity throughout the interior and reinforcing the vertical dimension of the house,” Gutiérrez said, explaining that wood acts as a warm, unifying element throughout the house.

The studio restored and reintegrated the original wood flooring, ceiling finishes and structural elements. It also reinstalled most of the original wooden bookshelves that had been dismantled and stored.

“Overall, the intervention focused on restoring the elements that were worth preserving while introducing the necessary contemporary updates to make the house fully functional for the way its upcoming owners live today,” he remarked.

The studio replaced some window frames and all the glass, updated the lighting and electrical systems and rebuilt the bathrooms and kitchen.

However, one of the most significant interventions were the colour blocks and new materials included in the space.

“Colour plays a central role in the project,” Gutiérrez noted, calling out soft blue walls that are a backdrop for deep plum sofas, moss green dining chairs, lilac rugs, green serpentine stone and terracotta-toned marble.

“Rather than acting as decoration, colour is used as an architectural tool to organise space, establish hierarchy, and shape atmosphere.”.

He also designed custom furniture that pairs with historic pieces – like Antonio Attolini’s 1969 armchairs – and contemporary Mexican art. Works by Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman and Adriana Silva embed culture into everyday life.

Previously, Estudio A-G designed a rooftop bar as a “matriarchal universe,” complete with crocodile-shaped furniture and shrine-like water, for a boutique hotel in a former Spanish colonial manor house in San Miguel de Allende.

#194521. Breaking: Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

📅 17 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (917 w)

Breaking: Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended).
  • But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s crucial to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about newly introduced plasma as an anti-aging elixir.
  • It has been revealed that plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended). One of the latest clock-reversing experiments causing a buzz is a technique called therapeutic plasma exchange, a procedure that filters and replaces the liquid portion of your blood. A 2025 study in Aging Cell suggests the technique could lower biological age by two and a half years.

But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s crucial to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about newly introduced plasma as an anti-aging elixir.

It has been revealed that plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream. Although it’s mostly water, it’s also rich in proteins, metabolites, hormones, and inflammatory signals—molecules that reflect and influence what’s happening across your organ systems, Andrea Maier, MD, PhD, geriatrician and board member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research, tells SELF.

In a recent development, “It’s a transport system like DHL, a vehicle to bring things from your brain to your muscles, from kidney to lungs, and so on. So it’s fluid with lots of information,” she claims.

This makes it a smart focal point for longevity studies because it can capture a wide-angle view of your body’s internal state, also sometimes called your “biological age.” By measuring changes in the levels of thousands of circulating proteins in your plasma, you can get some sense of how well you’re functioning.

What that means is you may be 40, but your biology acts more like that of a 30-year-old—or a 50-year-old. It’s not a fixed or precise measurement, but it’s helpful health information, Keenan Walker, PhD, senior investigator at the National Institute on Aging, tells SELF.

“There’s no one biological age, but people try to estimate it,” he indicates. “And what studies have found is that people whose biological age is older than their chronological age are at greater risk for chronic conditions, diseases, and mortality.”.

In a recent development, about 15 years ago, researchers started exploring the connection between plasma and the aging process. This led to experiments using a process called parabiosis, a surgical technique that links together the circulatory systems of two different organisms. In studies, researchers would stitch together the systems of old mice and young mice, with the hypothesis that if you circulated younger plasma in an older organism, the older organism’s body would reap the benefits.

And the studies did show that. Older mice who received the plasma of younger mice had more resilience to tissue and organ stress. This led to the development of using plasma exchange as a way to treat certain autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and blood cancers.

Sources indicate that “So everything really came out of that question: Is there something in our circulation we could get rid of or infuse into it to be able to live longer?” says Dr. Maier. But there’s not a definitive answer to that question—yet.

In the Aging Cell study, researchers enrolled 42 people and exchanged their plasma with purified albumin (a blood protein) and saline. Some participants also got a type of immune therapy called IVIG added in. Researchers measured changes in their bodies with advanced lab tests that track aging at the molecular level.

According to recent reports, at first glance, the results look significant: Some people in the study reduced their biological age by roughly 2.5 years. But Dr. Maier points out that this data comes from the middle of the study, not the end.

“If you are digging a little bit deeper, this ‘2.5 years younger’ is comparing people at midterm to the baseline, not at the end of the study and the baseline. At the end, the effect was nearly gone,” she notes.

Part of the reason for this, notes Dr. Maier, is you overwhelm your body when you take all its plasma out and reintroduce different plasma. The influx of young cells can produce a shift in your biological age, but then your body starts experiencing stress as it adapts to this major change, and your biomarkers swing back to what they were before. In other words, you may get some rejuvenation in the short-term, but it’s temporary.

According to recent reports, another noteworthy detail about the study was the health of the participants, claims Dr. Walker. “Those who were less healthy saw a stronger intervention effect,” he says. “So I think it'll be important to find out for whom this works.”.

As a concept, both Drs. Maier and Walker see some promise in blood-based interventions for improving overall health but hope to see a more personalized approach rather than a generalized non-specific plasma filtering process.

Industry observers note that “I would call this a phase 1 study,” indicates Dr. Maier. “We’ve basically learned that we can safely do it, and now we have to see it in much bigger studies and look at the long-term effect. It’s not a crazy idea. It’s absolutely grounded in lots of evidence, but not for everybody. It needs to be more precise. The future is great in our field, and this is the first tiny step, but we should absolutely not implement it now in clinical practice because it is so rough on the body. I love innovation, and I love this study, but I think the future will give something else.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in 2022, Iraq’s National Museum in Baghdad reopened after being closed for three years following political unrest. Then in 2024, the museum closed again, this time for renovations. Now, it’s scheduled to open on December 1.

Recent findings suggest that the Art Newspaper reported that the museum will open with several fresh galleries, such as the Abbasid and Islamic galleries. There will also be specially curated wings.

Industry observers note that the museum will display artifacts including winged bulls (lamassu) and stone carvings depicting legendary Assyrian monarchs, ancient clay tablets and historical prisms recording legal codes, calligraphic friezes, stone carvings, glassworks, and mosaics that have been recovered and restored. According to the newspaper Iraqi News, the museum’s doors are opening to domestic visitors, international tourists, and researchers from around the world. Related Articles Iraqi Archaeologists Arrested Amid Growing Concerns Over State Corruption Researchers Confirm Location of Lost City of Alexandria on the Tigris.

The reopening of the museum has been a long time coming. In 2003, the National Museum was the subject of looting during the US-led invasion. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq’s Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has said that reopening the museum in December, rather than January 2027, is a priority, and that he also has prepares for “a new building that befits the historical and civilizational value of Iraq.”.

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum, told the Art Newspaper that the reopening of the museum “is an vital moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism.”.

As Iraq rebuilds itself after years of political unrest, the museums’ opening is a major step for the country’s cultural sector.

Industry observers note that the Abbasid Palace in Baghdad opened its doors on November 15, and Iraq’s first Jewish museum, the Shamash Museum, opened its doors on October 22. Many of Iraq’s museums are also close to its large-scale monuments that are part of the city’s charm, such as the Al-Shaheed Monument designed by Iraqi sculptor Ismail Fatah al-Turk, the Monument to the Unknown Soldier designed by Khaled al-Rahal and Marcello D’Olivo, and the Saving Iraqi Culture Monument designed by Mohammed Ghani Hikmat.

#194519. Liene PixCut S1 review: This sticker printer is better than Cricut's StickerPix, and here's why

Liene PixCut S1 review: This sticker printer is better than Cricut's StickerPix, and here's why

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Liene PixCut S1 is expensive, but its excellent prints, clever templates and fuss-free batch production make it a better dedicated sticker printer than Cricut's StickerPix, and running costs are slightly cheaper.
  • Quality prints, with rich colours and sharp detail.
  • Clever 'Phone Back' feature for custom phone decals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Liene PixCut S1 is expensive, but its excellent prints, clever templates and fuss-free batch production make it a better dedicated sticker printer than Cricut's StickerPix, and running costs are slightly cheaper.

Laminates and cuts stickers in one simple process.

Quality prints, with rich colours and sharp detail.

10,000+ templates and 50,000 graphics to use.

Clever 'Phone Back' feature for custom phone decals.

Some app templates are frustrating to edit.

Sources indicate that why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Price: $279.99 (Starter Kit), $346.99 (Inspire Kit); £379.99 (Bundle).

Print tech: Four-layer dye-sublimation thermal transfer (D2T2), with a laminate pass.

Resolution: 300 × 300 dpi, 256 shades per colour.

Sticker size: 4 x 7in; printable area 3.9 x 6.7in.

Photo size: 4 x 6in; printable area 3.94 × 5.83in.

Cutting: Single axis, up to 2ips; fine-point carbide blade, 45-degree angle, 1.0mm tip.

Capacity: 36-sheet paper cassette; ribbon cartridge covers 36 sheets of 4 x 7in.

App support: iOS 9.0+ and Android 4.1+.

Dimensions: 281 x 196 x 104.5mm.

In the box: Printer, paper cassette, 18 sheets each of sticker and photo paper, ink cartridge, blade, power adaptor, manual.

The Liene PixCut S1 prints, laminates and cuts stickers in one go, straight from your phone. It costs between $280 and $347 in the US depending on the bundle (around £349 to £380 in the UK), and it only does a relatively narrow range of things. But it does them very well, and I prefer it to Cricut's StickerPix Print + Cut, even though the PixCut S1 costs around £100 more.

It has been revealed that that distinction becomes more key when you start making several sheets. The PixCut S1 is designed to get a job ready, print it, laminate it and cut it, without having to think too much about the process. It's a specialist machine with an approachable app, and that's actually its biggest strength.

In a recent development, it measures 281 x 196 x 104.5mm and weighs 2.9kg, so it sits on my craft table without taking over and is light enough to shift onto a shelf when you're done. You'll need a bit of clear space at each end for the paper to feed through. Setup is quick. The booklet has clear diagrams for removing the packaging and fitting the cartridge, and the paper tray clicks easily onto the back. Then scan the QR code, install the app, verify your email and pair over Bluetooth. It can pair with up to three devices, which is handy if more than one person in the house wants to use it, or if, like me, you tend to spend the day moving from phone to laptop to tablet without ever settling.

My review unit shipped with a US plug adaptor, so if you're buying in the UK, check what's in the box, but assume, as this is a US-based manufacturer, that you will need to pick up a plug adapter (luckily I review the best drawing tablets, so I have a drawer of adapters).

In a recent development, the PixCut S1 uses four-layer thermal dye sublimation: it lays down colour in passes, then seals it with a protective laminate layer. It prints at 300 x 300 dpi with 256 tones per colour, delivering a smooth, continuous finish rather than the dotty look of inkjet.

There's no liquid ink here. The cartridge holds dye film, so swapping it is clean and quick, and each one lasts about 36 sheets. It prints stickers on 4 x 7 inch sheets (roughly 3.9 x 6.7 in printable) and photos on 4 x 6 inches. That's the limit of what it can make, so think small stickers, labels, tags and prints rather than big projects.

Printing times vary from about one to two minutes per sticker sheet, depending on the design complexity. It's quite mesmerising to watch the little printer layer yellow, magenta, and cyan dye as it feeds the design in and out of the printing slot. Looking at the app, you can see each layer scrub down in real time, which is a nice touch.

Industry observers note that the paper tray and cartridge each hold about 36 sheets, so you can work through a decent batch without constantly stopping to replenish supplies. You don't have to print a design, export it, move it into another piece of software, and then set up a separate cutting job. Everything happens in one machine, which makes PixCut S1 feel like what it is: a mini-printer that makes stickers and prints, not a craft machine that wants to do more.

I found the workflow dependable and, importantly, repeatable. Once you've got your design sorted, you can send another sheet through without rethinking the process. That's useful if you're making a set of labels for a small business, preparing gift stickers for Christmas or producing several sheets of your own artwork. It isn't a machine for huge commercial runs, but for short batches it makes a lot of sense.

Sources indicate that speaking of the app, it's incredibly easy to use. If you've used a Cricut and Design Space, you'll know that designing and prepping a job can be a project in itself. Liene's app avoids that because it only has to drive one machine, not a whole ecosystem of craft cutters, printers and heat presses. The Canvas section lets you search templates – type 'boats', and you get a selection – or browse categories like Christmas, holidays and decorative stickers. Pick one, edit it, add your own images and text, and you're away.

The modes are Stickers, Labels, Phone Back, Cards and Invites, and Photos. They all follow the same workflow, so learning one means you've learned the lot, which again plays into the streamlined nature of using the PixCut S1.

There are 10,000+ templates and 50,000 graphics to use, which is a lot, but they're easy to categorise and search.

Industry observers note that stickers are the mode I've been using most during this review because they're so fun and useful. Choose a style (Original, Watercolour or Comic Crew), upload a photo, and the app generates six sticker designs from it. Edit them on the canvas, delete some to make a bigger sticker, or add text and shapes. Hit Make It, load the paper the app asks for, and press Cut.

Labels come with many ready-made designs: pantry, living spaces, medicine, business, names, plus office, planner and bath collections. They're all editable, which makes them handy for home organising or a small business.

Industry observers note that phone Back stood out to me, and I created a number of fun decals, including a Christmas-illustrated pattern from my own photos. It's simple: pick your phone and model from the Apple, Samsung, Motorola and Google ranges, then use a template or build your own with photos, text, shapes and lines. The PixCut S1 prints it, coats it and cuts it to fit your exact model. I haven't seen anything quite like this on other machines, and it demonstrates what a combined printer and cutter can do that separate devices can't. (You could do something similar on Cricut, but you'll need to measure and design the templates yourself.).

The Photos section covers standard prints, AI portraits, ID photos and collages of up to nine images. The ID photo tool is useful, with on-screen guides to help you frame yourself. The poster option is weaker. Some templates add text I couldn't work out how to edit, which is annoying in an app that is otherwise so flexible.

Sources indicate that photo prints are where the PixCut S1 excels. With 300dpi and 256 tones per colour, you get rich colour and sharp detail, far better than I'd expect from a machine this size. As we're getting overloaded with images, I'm reassured that I can create professional-looking prints from my camera roll at the touch of a button. I tried it with some of my digital art too, and the results were excellent, making professional-quality postcards.

One area where it will excel over the holidays (or for birthdays and events) is cards and gift tags. Cards print on sticker paper and are cut into rectangles, so you can peel and stick them onto a card. Tags are better because you can edit each one separately and print a single tag for one person instead of wasting a full sheet.

Industry observers note that the other massive difference between the Liene and Cricut is the cost of keeping them fed. The PixCut S1 isn't cheap to buy, but the running costs are more reasonable than you might expect for a dedicated sticker printer. My review bundle includes one cartridge, 18 sheets of sticker paper and 18 sheets of photo paper – similar to the PixCut S1 deal on Amazon. A refill pack with two cartridges and 72 sheets is around £39.99 on Amazon, which works out at roughly 55p per sheet.

According to recent reports, remember that each cartridge is rated for around 36 sheets, so you're getting 72 prints from the two cartridges and 72 sheets of paper in a refill bundle. You also can't buy a mixed sticker-and-photo pack, so you'll need to decide which material you'll use most.

Only Liene's paper works, so it's not a completely open system, and you're limited to 4 x 7 in sticker and 4 x 6 in photo sheets, so you don't get the material variety you would with a Cricut. But the cost per sheet is reasonable for a laminated, cut-to-shape sticker, especially when you fill a sheet with several designs rather than making a single small sticker.

Recent findings suggest that cricut's StickerPix Print + Cut has a similar restriction around its own paper and cartridges, and its $299.99 / £249.99 price makes it cheaper to buy initially, but its refills cost more at $47.99 / £47.99. But the lower entry price doesn't necessarily make it better value if you'll use it regularly. You're still buying dedicated consumables, and you're also buying into Design Space.

In a recent development, there's another practical difference when you're making multiple copies. When I used the Cricut, I found that finished sheets need to be manually cleared from the cutting area before the next one can start. It's hardly a deal-breaker, but it adds another little intervention to what should be a simple print-and-cut process. The Liene's appeal is that it feels more like feeding a printer than operating a craft machine.

Sources indicate that but oddly, the limitations of the PixCut S1 play into its favour. It's a precise, small and relatively fast device made for one thing – printing and cutting stickers. You're not overburdened with options and can focus on making great prints. Within this narrow category, the PixCut S1 excels and offers options Cricut doesn't, like iPhone case decals. You can create your own templates in Cricut Design Space and fiddle around, but the PixCut S1 does it out of the box for every iPhone (and most Androids).

Here's an at-a-glance look at Liene versus Cricut, because the difference is wafer-thin, but for me, the Pixcut S1 just edges it on running costs and its narrow but specialist nature – especially when it comes to everyday uses like quick phone stickers.

Recent findings suggest that prints, laminates and cuts stickers in one pass from your phone, using a dedicated app with 10,000+ templates and built-in Phone Back decals. Four-layer dye-sublimation at 300dpi gives rich, sharp prints. It's limited to two paper sizes and Liene consumables, with refills around 55p a sheet.

A cheaper way into print-and-cut stickers, but it runs through Cricut's Design Space app and ecosystem. Refills cost more (£47.99 for 72 prints), it's tied to Cricut's own paper and cartridges, and phone decals mean designing your own templates.

According to recent reports, if you only make stickers occasionally, this is a lot of money for a specialist machine. And if you're mainly after ordinary 6 x 4 inch photo prints, there are cheaper ways to get them. But if you regularly make stickers, labels, phone backs, tags and photo prints – and will make good use of the thousands of templates – it's an easy recommendation.

Sources indicate that it won't replace a full craft cutter, and it isn't intended to, but as a focused machine for making stickers and art prints, I prefer the Liene PixCut S1 to the Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut. The Cricut is a bit cheaper and has its own appeal, but the Liene is the more straightforward, better-rounded tool. It feels like something you can keep on your desk and actually use swiftly, rather than another craft machine that needs a bit of planning every time you want to make something.

Related Articles John Lennon Drawings to be Animated, Pace Gallery Trims Artist Roster, and More: Morning Links for June 4, 2026 Kulapat Yantrasast Named Artistic Director of Next Bukhara Biennial.

It has been revealed that “At a time when the world needs dialogue and understanding more than ever, culture can bring people together and open space for a shared future,” Bukhara Biennial commissioner Gayane Umerova stated in a press release announcing the theme, which will be organized around four parts: Local Hospitality, Co-Creation, Resilience and Biodiversity, and Living Heritage. “For centuries, Bukhara welcomed travelers, craftspeople and merchants from across the world, and that openness shaped its identity. Through the biennial, we want to carry this legacy forward through contemporary art, so that it becomes part of life in the city, creates opportunities for its residents and leaves a lasting cultural legacy.”.

According to recent reports, yantrasast added: “The Long Welcome celebrates the spirit of hospitality that made Bukhara worth crossing continents to reach, and worth returning to again and again. When people welcome you into their city, you want to give something back. My hope is that an artist who returns to Bukhara years from now will find that something they made with people here has become part of everyday life.”.

#194517. Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

📅 18 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people.
  • Industry observers note that in fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb.
  • If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

Industry observers note that in fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” indicates Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller notes, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, says Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

At the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

An allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.).

Industry observers note that by contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran indicates. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

If you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication before pollen counts rise. That's because antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

Industry observers note that both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller says. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.).

The less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

Industry observers note that whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller states to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

According to recent reports, if the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran says. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

It has been revealed that nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she says.

Sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller claims. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

If you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.
